Nice , soothing Monday puzzle. Good way to end the weekend!

Regarding TAS:

When our kids were little, we had a nanny from England who tried to teach our little ones to be thankful, by making them say "TA" when they received something.  The wife and I were scratching our heads over this mystery word, which eventually we figured out.

We had to inform the nanny that no one says "TA" in America.

Sam may be confused about the spelling of NEAPOLITAN, but Neapolis does mean "new city" in Greek.

I'll also mention that the clue/answer agreement rule allows for exceptions based on the meaning of the words.  Since "TORTS" is a single law class, the clue can be singular without breaking any rules.  (I'm not saying Sam didn't know this, but I wanted to point out that this pairing is not just some random outlier.)
The fact about tepidly is a great one. A brilliant word and often under used. Really enjoyed this one and came in with 17 mins on the clock!
Regarding 30A, this is not correct citation form; you always give the last name of the author, followed by the initial(s) of the first (and second) name(s), quoth I.

Fine Monday puzzle with a simple but elegant theme, which should enhance the experience if not speed the solve.
Thanks! 

I do take issue (nit?) with Sam's "the entries at 13-, 29- and 37-Across cast “shadow boxes” — i.e., shaded squares — into the entries below them, following the angle of the SUN at 1A." They do not follow the angle, which varies for each themer: all of the shadows are one square to the right.

Really top notch Monday and interesting, clever theme.

For anyone who hasn’t tried Mondays with across only, it’s really a fascinating way to look at how your brain and common words work. I had everything but the bottom left and the revealer (I thought; I had ARNESS before ARNETT; MRT looked like it would work fine but should have known POES wouldn’t be there especially with POE in the grid).

I got the theme with TREE first, which I thought was odd in two places. I hadn’t noticed HAT. But what was really funny is I did think of FAWNING OVER first but didn’t use it because I had GOAT going down instead of N for the GNAT; and was thinking how odd it was that it had AWNING in it, but still didn’t connect it.

But the SW was most interesting. I had _A_M_D for “made waves” (my A was wrong but that’s because I naturally had OSWALD before OSWEGO especially because it was in a recent puzzle). I thought of CALMED first—oddly the opposite of made waves. Then DAMMED which made sense. Then when I got TEPIDLY  I finally settled on PALMED as in waved hello and goodbye. My other misread on acrosses was REMOTE then SEDATE for the retreat. Any way, no way I was going to get the revealer without help and all those wrong guesses (and would never have guessed an X for _ER.) So I finally gave in and looked at the downs.

So that was a 30 min Monday for me but it made it really interesting and a brain teaser, I really recommend it for anyone bored and sailing through early week puzzles!
I totally missed the SUN! How cool was that? Should have been highlighted or animated or something, at least at the end.
TIL how to correctly spell that particular ice cream flavour.

67A across really resonated; I literally just got home from a screening of YOU HAD TO BE THERE, about the 1972 Toronto  production of GODSPELL which launched so very many comedy, acting, performing and directing legends, including Victor Garber, Eugene Levy, Gilda Radner, Andrea Martin, Paul Shaffer, Martin Short, and Don Scardino.

My hours of NYT Crossword solving really paid off for me this weekend.

This weekend was "Moose Madness" in Grand Marais.  Part of it is there are posters around town with facts about moose, with one letter highlighted.  We were told there were six signs, and that if we could get them and unscramble the word, we'd each get five "moose bucks" to spend at one of about a dozen stores in town.

We were also told the word was related to moose.

We found signs with the following letters:  PLDW.  At this point I knew the answer, and was not surprised to hear that the final two letters were A and E.

So we get home, my wife and I and two grand kids, and they sat down at the table to work out the word.  I told them I already knew it (as many of you probably do as well).  

My wife tentatively said DEWLAP, but she thought it was a joke.  I confirmed it.

Price of NYT Games subscription:  about 4 dollars a month.  The adulation of your grandkids:  priceless.

Beyond the shadow of a doubt, this puzzle was a lovely way to spend some time on a serene Sunday afternoon.  

Thank you, Michele.  You put together a Monday puzzle that was easy, with clues that were imaginative! (Not fawning about the awning, but not said tepidly.)

(One tree pun is fine, but I'll be sycamore of them.)

Your AWNING is our markiza. The etymology of the word is quite interesting and related to your marquee. Apparently in olden times marquises (the high-ranked nobles) often served as military commanders. On campaign a marquis would sleep in a tent distinguished from those of lesser men by a linen canopy over the entrance. Both the Polish "markiza" and your "marquee" arose from the association between marquises and the canopies of their tents.

Hopefully one day I can solve entire puzzle without looking up the answers.

But I am glad that my skills are gradually improving especially when I start to recognize some words that are repeatedly used, like "SINEW" today (which I believe was an answer to two of last week's puzzles?).

I also thank NYT crossword puzzle helping me to get familiarized with random US facts. I just learned another river in NY besides Hudson (OSWEGO) or the new super market brand (IGA) and the triple colored ice cream was not napolitan but NEAPOLITAN! I thought it was named after Napoleon :)

By the way, i bet there are some lawyers here, but i also bet most of the rest are not 100% sure what TORTS are. I remember learning about tort law via the classic case of the slug in the bottle. 

In short, two Scottish ladies went to a cafe. One ordered drinks for both of them. The one who didn’t order found a snail in her ginger beer and tried to sue the ginger beer manufacturer, Mr Stevenson. He claimed she couldn’t sue them because she wasn’t the one who ordered the drinks, and therefore she had no contract with him. But the judge ruled that he still had a “duty of care” to her, contract or no contract, and he had been negligent. He had committed a tort: a wrong that isn’t governed by a contract. 

(Now all you lawyers can tell me how i got this wrong…🤓)

Only just now saw that the SHADOWBOXES were all words in the “shade” of the actual words themselves, one line below and to the right. (Kind of skipped over Sam’s description of that in the column — oops!). Very impressive construction, Ms. Govier!

Well, let's see.  The HAT casts a shadow on the...HAT?!  The TREE casts a shadow on the...TREE?!  And the AWNING casts a shadow on the...AWNING?!

This is all very odd.  Isn't the HAT casting a shadow on, say, the TENNIS PLAYER?  Isn't the TREE casting a shadow on, say, the FORESTER?  And isn't the AWNING casting a shadow on, say, the FIFTH AVENUE APARTMENT DOORMAN?

I had fun with this because I was completely in sunlight.  Once I had HAT and once I had SHADOW BOXES, I absolutely knew ahead of time that the other two would be TREE and AWNING.  Yes, AWNING!  Immediately!

This is because I'm a born and bred New Yorker.  I don't know where y'all get your shade in, say, rural Montana.  I think you have eaves and overhangs and porches.  Also, you plant TREEs right outside your front door and maybe your back door too.  But here in NYC, we have AWNINGS.  Why, if you're a Fifth Avenue residential building and you don't have an AWNING, they'll kick you right off the street.  "You don't have an AWNING???  I think we need to talk."

As odd as the conceit of the puzzle was, guessing the shadow-inducing objects was fun for me.  I had a good time.

@Canard Baht certainly does have a meaning in English. The Merriam-Webster dictionary defines it as 'the basic monetary unit of Thailand.' The clue calls for Thai currency units. The dictionary says the plural form is 'baht also bahts'. Although the plural form isn't used in Thailand, for the purposes of the NYT puzzle, it's not incorrect.

@Andrzej. But they ARE wrong grammatically.  It's the same as Japanese Yen or South African Rand.  You don't say Yens or Rands at a bank exchange counter.  It’s not a big deal to me, but the NY Times prides itself on accuracy, and any future use of "Yens" will be called out too.

@Michael

Some (not all) dictionaries list "bahts" as an alternative to "baht", but it seems ridiculous to me. The English language has no trouble treating "yen" as both singular and plural, presumably because that was how the Japanese themselves used the word.

@CB

The Cambridge dictionary lists it as baht, plural baht. The word "bahts" might exist in some dictionaries, but there is no situation where saying "bahts" would be preferable to "baht".

@nkg

I really don't get why this particular case of English doing weird things with plurals of foreign words is ridiculous. NEAPOLITAN is a Greek-based demonym meaning "of the new city."  "New city" is νέα πόλη (nea poli) in Greek, and Napoli, Italy was originally Neapolis.  

The S at the end and the I at the end in Italian probably made early cartographers think the name was a plural; hence, we have "Naples" in English.  But what's a Naple, anyway?

Interestingly, Nablus (in the West Bank) is a cognate.  As in the next hamlet to my own Haverstraw, which is New City (which is not actually a city).  Carthage, Newcastle, and dozens of others share a similar meaning.
